newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Belgian GIB swings back to profit in 1996.
newsitem.headline: Belgian GIB swings back to profit in 1996.

text.p: Belgian retail group GIB said on Thursday it swung into profit in 1996 after a hefty loss the year before due to exceptionals on the sale of its U.S. home-improvement unit Handy Andy.
GIB made a group net profit of 3.39 billion Belgian francs ($97.7 million) after a 4.39 billion loss in 1995, when the group announced an extraordinary loss of 5.5 billion
Consolidated turnover edged down to 216.56 billion francs from 227.78 billion, but on a like-for-like basis it rose slightly.
GIB is Belgium's second largest retail group after Delhaize in terms of turnover. GIB, whose financial year ends on January 31, said its 1996 figures were provisional.
Its flagship GB supermarket unit maintained market share for the second year. Its sales rose 2.2 percent, and sales of food products rose 3.3 percent.
GB has achieved a 22 percent improvement in productivity in its stores since 1994.
GIB's supermarkets and hypermarkets division accounts for 67 percent of total group sales.
The group said it was still seeking a partner for its department store chain Inno, but with no luck so far.

"It will take time to find Inno a partner. One day we'll find one, but I can't say when -- the big magazine chains (in Europe) are not really expanding," GIB's chief executive officer Diego du Monceau told a news conference.
GIB said Inno ended the financial year at breakeven, though it made an operating profit. Despite a sluggish textiles market sales edged up 0.5 percent to 8.4 billion francs.
Asked about the outlook generally for the GIB group in 1997, Du Monceau said it was too early to make a forecast.
"It depends on the economy, the weather, a pickup in consumption at (burger unit) Quick Restaurants," he said, noting "we have no big problem companies at the moment".

GIB plans to invest seven billion Belgian francs in 1997, and its priorities for the year include reinforcing the competitiveness of its super- and hypermarkets, redefining its local neighbourhood store concept, and developing GB's commercial agreement with France's Promodes.
It also wanted to continue the expansion of its European do-it-yourself (DIY) operations, to continue the recovery at its U.S. DIY unit Scotty's, and to make Quick more competitive.

European DIY sales rose 0.7 percent in 1996 despite poor weather. Scotty's reported an increase of 3.1 percent in dollar sales, which, combined with careful cost control, helped the chain to double operating profit to $12.5 million, GIB said. ($ = 34.69 Belgian Francs)
